1. FROM MY DESK

Warren Buffett has stepped down from the company he built more than half a century ago, bringing an extraordinary era at (Berkshire Hathaway) to a close. His son Howie is taking over as chairman, completing a succession plan years in the making. But his appointment also tells us what Buffett fears could happen to Berkshire without him.

Howie is an unconventional choice to help lead a $1 trillion conglomerate. He never graduated from college and has spent much of his career farming and running a charitable foundation. But his father has long seen him as uniquely suited to protect Berkshire's culture and sprawling structure from pressure for change, as questions grow about its enormous cash pile, its lagging stock and whether its collection of businesses should remain intact.
Krystal Hur and Gregory Zuckerman unpack the historic move, and we break down five key things to know about Berkshire's new chairman.

President Trump said the U.S. and Denmark reached an agreement that allows for more American forces in Greenland.
Some Republicans are distancing themselves from Trump on key policies like tariffs and the Iran war, a sign they believe his stances are hurting their election prospects.
Paramount is in advanced talks with California officials aimed at resolving the antitrust lawsuit that stands in the way of its deal to acquire  Warner Bros. Discovery.

A volatile week on Wall Street ended quietly with the Dow Jones Industrial Average falling for a third straight week, while the Nasdaq eked out a gain.
The buyers of the Los Angeles Lakers expect to nearly triple the team's valuation to at least $30 billion within a decade.
4. READ IT HERE FIRST
Venezuela's opposition leader is planning a high-stakes return from exile.

Nine months after escaping Venezuela in disguise to accept the Nobel Peace Prize, María Corina Machado is preparing her next move. In a rare interview in Panama City, Machado detailed her high-stakes plan to go back home, reignite a peaceful grassroots movement and press for elections to eventually dethrone the U.S.-backed interim government. But her return faces resistance from some Trump administration officials who fear her presence could upend fragile stability and disrupt lucrative oil deals. Vera Bergengruen details Machado's "shadow embassy," her tech-driven transition strategy and the debate over Venezuela's political future.
Law firms are facing an awkward problem: Senior partners refuse to retire.

With roughly a third of U.S. lawyers aged 55 or older, elite law firms built on cradle-to-grave partnerships are confronting a growing bottleneck at the top. At some firms, aging partners who work well into their 80s are blocking younger talent from leading practices and securing major cases. The pressure is mounting as aggressive competitors embark on an unprecedented poaching spree. To make way for the next generation without losing key clients, major firms like Latham & Watkins and Debevoise are hiring specialized consultants to coax veterans into second careers. Erin Mulvaney explores how law firms are trying to solve their retirement crisis.

8. THE NUMBER

That's about the percentage of Net-a-Porter's customer base driving nearly 50% of its revenue. To turn around the struggling business, CEO Heather Kaminetsky zeroed in on those high-spending shoppers, wooing them with direct emails, exclusive country-estate dinners and custom requests like getting a designer to make a single pair of sold-out leopard pants for a customer. The intense focus on top clientele is paying off: Sales rose 4.3% last quarter, while average order values over the past year topped $1,000.
